extracted.intended_audience: early-modern natural philosophers, anatomists, microscopists, metallurgists, and alum/refinery craftsmen (readers of Philosophical Transactions)
extracted.subtask_description: Detailed, practical instructions and observational-method notes for (1) refining gold and silver by several historical techniques (parting with aquafortis, the test, almond furnace/sweep, mercury/amalgamation) and (2) producing alum from mined mineral; also includes microscopy/anatomical observation methods. The page gives recipes, apparatus design, operational schedules, and quality-control signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parting with aquafortis — recipe and apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Parting is done with aquafortis, which the refiners make thus: take of saltpetre 3 lb. Dantzic vitriol 2 lb.; bruise and mix in a mortar, put into long-neck earthen vessels (long-necks) and arrange them in the furnace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fill many long-necks, place them in ranges at above Q inches apart on iron bars, close sides with bricks, leave upper arches open for access; receivers (glass or German pots) must be well luted to the necks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lute composition for sealing receivers
rubrics_metrics.description: The lute is made of good loam, with some horse-dung and a little colcothar (though the two former do well).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work and apply the lute well to ensure receivers are sealed; good luting especially required on the two upper receivers in long distillation columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heating schedule for long-neck distillation
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a gentle charcoal fire under the pots for 3 hours, then increase for 3 hours more; about the 7th hour make a vehement hot fire for 4 hours and cast in well-dried billets to finish the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually performed once in 24 hours (sometimes twice); separate receivers carefully next morning. If vitriol is not of proper quality, the water will be weaker and spoil the product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distillation in cast-iron-pot 'alembic' arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative: distil 100 lb. in a cast-iron pot placed at the top of a 2-yard-high furnace with an earthen head dividing into three branches fitted with rows of glass bodies (globular midsections) luted together toward a receiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This saves many long-necks and permits use of a smaller fire (Newcastle coal); only the lowermost receiver needs to be opened frequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purification of aquafortis by 'fixes'
rubrics_metrics.description: After distillation, put aquafortis into an earthen pot and add 1–2 pennyweights of fine silver (fixes) per pound of aquafortis; in 4 hours this purges dirt and makes it fit for parting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This treatment readies aquafortis for parting operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parting procedure and behaviour indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Place small pieces of metal into tapering glass charged with aquafortis, heat gently; bubbles rise, water may run over; let stand a night with gentle heat and pour off water impregnated with silver next morning; gold lies as black dirt to be washed and melted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the water boils over it can penetrate bricks/wood; repeat pouring/washing 5–6 times to separate salt from gold; greenness of the water indicates copper content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making and using the test (the 'test' method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make an iron oval mould filled with fine powder of bone-ashes moistened with lixivium, press smooth, leaving a cavity for melted silver; set annealing 24 hours; place in a chimney with strong blast (bellows), cover silver with billets of barked oak and begin the blast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead (soap of metals) and copper will melt and rise; the refiner stirs with a long iron rod toward a slit to run off baser metals; separation is made in 2–3 hours; lead fumes fly off; good tests serve two or three firings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of 'driving' and when to add lead in the test
rubrics_metrics.description: If the lead is gone before all the copper, the metal rises in small red fiery bubbles and 'drives'; add more lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The force of the blast moves upper metal to the lower side of the test and promotes running over; when fully refined silver looks like pure quicksilver and is cooled and beaten to a round before melting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melting-pots handling and anti-cracking practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Melting-pots are set in a wind furnace, surrounded with coal and covered with an iron cap; if any dross throw in tincal to collect it; melting-pots are never burned but only dried and will last a whole day if not allowed to cool; if they cool they crack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep pots hot; add tincal to collect dross; avoid cooling to prevent cracking and loss of pot life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Almond furnace / sweep method for separating metals
rubrics_metrics.description: Beat cinders, melting-pot parts, tests, brick and hard bodies into small pieces; use a wooden round instrument and water in a tub to wave and separate lighter matter; furnace is brick (6 ft high x 4 ft wide x 2 ft thick) with holes for bellows and receiver; anneal furnace night before, then run continuously for 3 days and nights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metal will begin to run after 8–10 hours; use slag to give fusion if hard to flux; stop passage-holes with cinders to keep heat; stinking blue smoke results and bystanders are affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mercury (quicksilver) amalgamation method
rubrics_metrics.description: Put dust/fillings into a hand-mill with quicksilver and grind to form an amalgam, then wash with water carried off by a small quill; put amalgam into an iron bolt-head set in the fire with an iron neck and receiver to distil off the mercury, leaving gold and silver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by small workers/goldsmiths for filings and dust; mercury distillation must be fitted with receiver attached to the iron neck.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovering silver from silver-water and making verditer
rubrics_metrics.description: Pour silver-water into large wooden washing-bowls lined with rosin and pitch, fitted with copper plates; working the water on softer copper deposits silver as fine sand which is washed, dried and melted. For verditer, mix the copper-water with 100 lb whiting and stir daily until pale, dry on chalk in sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If copper plates contain brass/shruff metal they will gather little silver; the water from verditer is boiled to water-gruel thickness and redistilled to make double aquafortis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'fixes' and repeated treatments to remove impurities
rubrics_metrics.description: After parting/distillation, wash and repeat treatments (pouring, washing 5–6 times) to separate salts from gold and render material fit to melt into ingots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated washing and parting steps are necessary to avoid contamination of final metal by salts or copper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting alum mineral and mine conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Alum stone is found between Scarborough and the river Tees and near Preston; best when the mine lies deep and is indifferently well moistened with springs; a dry mine is not good and too much moisture cankers the stone making it nitrous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid too-dry or overly-wet mines; doggers and snake-stones are inferior; begin workings on a declivity for water supply and to save carriage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calcining alum mineral and fire management
rubrics_metrics.description: Calcine mineral with cinders of Newcastle coal, wood and furzes in heaps (about 1½ ft thick, 2 yd broad, 10 yd long) and kindle fires so they burn through the heap; wind can hurt calcination by forcing fire too quickly leaving black or red pieces; slow, self-passing fire yields white mineral which gives best liquor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage the fire so it advances evenly; stage heaps to control calcination; incorrect calcining leads to poor liquor and slam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential leaching in pits and liquor flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Put calcined mineral into water pits supported with wood frames (approx. 10 yd long x 5 yd broad x 5 ft deep) with a current; virgin liquor is pumped into a pit of mineral and then pumped sequentially through four pits of mineral before the liquor goes to the boiling-house; each pit steep about 24 hours so mineral passes four days overall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pumping liquor through several pits concentrates it; last pit is always fresh mineral; poor calcining or bad mineral reduces yield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring liquor 'weight' and interpreting yields
rubrics_metrics.description: Virgin liquor often gains 2 lb in first pit, 5 lb in second, 8 lb in third and 12 lb in last; sometimes only 6–7 lb depending on mineral and calcining; liquor of 7–8 lb often yields more alum than 10–12 lb because latter may contain nitre and slam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume heavier liquor always yields better alum; watch for contamination introduced by the last pit (nitre/slam).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizing and handling 'slam' (impurities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Slam is perceived by redness of the liquor when it comes from the pit (caused by bad mineral or over/under-calcining); in the settler slam sinks to the bottom becoming muddy and dark; whitest liquor from pits is best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using liquor high in slam; if liquor is nitrous/red use more kelp-lees and urine later to correct, but overall good calcining prevents slam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kelp (tangle ash) production and its role
rubrics_metrics.description: Kelp is made from tangle seaweed, dried and burned to ashes, steeped in water to produce lees; kelp-lees (about a hogshead for a boiler) are used in boiling to reduce weight and help cast off nitre and slam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kelp-lees act like yeast in good liquor; in poor (nitrous) liquor they have less effect and more/stronger lees are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing urine quality used in alum process
rubrics_metrics.description: Because country people sometimes mix urine with sea-water, test urine by adding it to some boiling liquor: good urine will 'work like yeast' in boiling liquor, whereas mixed (bad) urine will not behave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best urine is from poor labouring people who drink little strong liquor; urine is used to cast off slam and to keep kelp-lees from hardening alum too much.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boiling-house practice, boilers and 'mothers' reuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Boiling pans of lead (approx. 9 ft long x 5 ft broad x 2½ ft deep) are set on iron plates; once alum is made save 'mothers' (liquor in which alum shoots) to fill two-thirds of boilers and add one-third fresh liquor; while boiling fill up every two hours as liquor wastes ~4 inches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mothers to speed boiling; repeated topping and monitoring avoid long re-heating; good liquor appears greasy on top, nitrous appears thick/muddy/red.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boiling schedule and use of kelp-lees and urine in coolers
rubrics_metrics.description: Boil to about 36 lb, then add kelp-lees to reduce to about 27 lb; draw into a settler for ~2 hours; scoop into a cooler and add ~20 gallons of urine (more or less per liquor quality); in temperate weather liquor stands 4 days in cooler for alum to strike (longer in hot weather).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If liquor remains in cooler over 4 days it turns to copperas; hot weather lengthens cooling; frosty weather causes early hardening that traps slam and nitre, making fouler alum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weather effects on crystallization and washing outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: In temperate weather alum gathers in about 4 days; in hot weather it takes longer; in frosty weather cold strikes the alum too soon preventing nitre/slam settling, producing more but fouler alum requiring more washing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time cooling to weather; expect trade-offs between quantity and purity under different conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopy: specimen freshness and handling for spermatic observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe semen from healthy men immediately post-ejection (not long-preserved or corrupted); in freshly ejected fluid many animalcules are visible moving; in thicker (coarser) parts animalcules are quiescent; addition of rainwater quickly causes death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Microscope observation should use fresh samples and note differences between thicker and thinner fractions; some animalcules persist up to ~36 hours in a glass tube but many become moribund or die.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopy: storage, lifespan and medium effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Portions stored in a glass tube (1/12th of an ounce) show most animalcules dead after 30–36 hours though some moribund remain; adding rainwater or other fluids can hasten death; lymph from coitus exhibits fewer animalcules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document storage conditions and any additives; use comparative tests (rainwater, saliva, pituita) to demonstrate viability and existence of vessels/structures in semen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation and reporting of anatomical figures and labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures are labeled with letters (A, B, C etc.) and text provides explicit mapping: e.g., 'In fig. 1. pi. 13, A is the right kidney, B the left; C the middle part conjoining both kidneys; ... PQ pelvis ... RR the two ureters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing dissection observations label parts clearly and provide explanatory caption mapping letters to anatomical structures; indicate anomalies (double ureters etc.) and how specimens were prepared (inflation, blowing into cavities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical technique: inflation/blowing to reveal cavities and vessels
rubrics_metrics.description: Blowing into glandulae renales/gland cavities and inflating pelvis reveals cavities and connections to veins; e.g., blowing emptied cavities into two veins demonstrating which veins they open into.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use careful inflation/blowing to trace drains; record where vessels enter larger veins; note relative sizes and any duplications (double ureters) and their insertions into bladder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative animal sampling and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe semen and lymph from different animals (rabbits, dogs, cats) and stages (coitus, immediately post-ejection) and compare animalcule abundance and behaviour; draw and transmit delineations of observed forms (figs. 5–12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record species, method of collection, approximate counts (relative to sand grains), and morphological notes (head, trunk, tail motion).
